name: Gause's Law
statement: Two species competing for the same limiting resource cannot stably coexist.
meaning: If two species use a limiting resource in exactly the same way — occupying an identical ecological niche — one will always be at least slightly more efficient. That small edge compounds until the less-efficient species is driven out. Perfect ecological equivalents cannot indefinitely share the same environment; coexistence requires that they differ in some meaningful way.
mechanism: Under constant conditions with one limiting resource, the superior competitor draws the shared resource down below the level the inferior one needs, excluding it. When species partition the resource — using different foods, microhabitats, or times — competition relaxes and both persist. The upshot, 'one niche, one species', bounds the number of coexisting species by the number of distinct limiting resources.

examples.text: Grown together on the same food, Paramecium aurelia and P. caudatum could not coexist — aurelia recovered and drove caudatum to extinction through resource competition. But P. caudatum and P. bursaria coexisted by occupying different parts of the culture tube, illustrating niche partitioning.

Galápagos finch species with differing beak sizes exploit different seed sizes, reducing overlap and permitting coexistence — the textbook field case of resource partitioning that lets close competitors share an island.

Hutchinson's 1961 puzzle: many phytoplankton species coexist in a seemingly uniform water column competing for the same few resources, which the principle says should be impossible — the canonical challenge to a strict reading.

variants.name: Niche partitioning
variants.text: The escape route from exclusion: when competitors differ in resource use, habitat, or timing, they occupy distinct niches and can coexist — the mechanism that reconciles the principle with real biodiversity.

variants.name: The paradox of the plankton
variants.text: Hutchinson's counterpoint (1961): real communities sustain far more coexisting competitors than the principle allows, resolved by never reaching equilibrium — environmental fluctuation interrupts exclusion before it completes.

whyItMatters: It is a cornerstone of community ecology, giving a crisp theoretical account of when competitors can and cannot share an environment and underwriting the whole idea of the ecological niche. Its very tidiness makes its exceptions instructive — the ways real ecosystems evade it reveal how coexistence actually works.

working.lead: Look for the difference that allows coexistence
working.text: when similar species persist together, expect a niche axis — food, space, or time — along which they differ, rather than true ecological identity.

working.lead: Treat it as an equilibrium benchmark
working.text: the strict prediction holds under constant conditions; real coexistence often depends on the system never settling to equilibrium.
because an unmeasured niche difference can almost always be invoked, guard against making the principle unfalsifiable in the field.

limits: Real ecosystems routinely show more coexisting competitors than the 'one resource, one species' bound predicts — the paradox of the plankton is the canonical counterexample. The strict principle holds only under idealised, constant, single-resource, equilibrium conditions; in the real world, spatial and temporal heterogeneity, disturbance, predation, and multiple co-limiting resources all enable coexistence. Because it is easy to rescue by invoking an unmeasured niche difference, some critics regard it as bordering on unfalsifiable in field settings — better treated as a theoretical benchmark than an ironclad law.
misreadings: It does not say competitors can never coexist — only that complete competitors, identical in resource use under constant conditions, cannot. Nearly all real coexisting species differ along some niche axis, which is exactly what the principle predicts. The phenomenon was demonstrated by Gause; the name 'competitive exclusion principle' and its crisp phrasing came later from Hardin.
origin: Demonstrated experimentally by the Soviet biologist Georgy Gause with Paramecium, published in 'The Struggle for Existence' (1934), building on the Lotka–Volterra competition models and earlier ideas from Joseph Grinnell. The name 'competitive exclusion principle' and the phrase 'complete competitors cannot coexist' were coined by Garrett Hardin in Science (1960).
